U.S. last-mile delivery prices rose 10.5% year over year in the third quarter, three times the 3.5% increase in consumer prices, according to a new quarterly index that logistics provider GEODIS launched this week.
What’s Related
The U.S. Final Mile Index tracks prices for two types of delivery that shippers often budget for separately. It covers parcel deliveries to households and local freight deliveries to businesses . The first edition also covers diesel prices, driver conditions, cargo theft and delivery performance.
How it works
GEODIS uses two U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price indexes, one for couriers and messengers and the other for local general freight trucking . It sets both series to 100 in 2019 and gives them equal weight. Together, they reached 149.8 in the third quarter, putting delivery prices 49.8% above the 2019 baseline. Consumer prices rose 30.8% over the same stretch, according to GEODIS.
The index gives shippers a benchmark for reviewing carrier rate increases or building a transportation budget. Because the headline number gives parcel and local trucking prices equal weight, a shipper that sends mostly packages may get a more relevant comparison from the parcel figures. A business that relies on local freight deliveries can look at the trucking figures separately.
RELATED: Delivery Reliability Now Matters as Much as Speed, Survey Finds
Fuel and missed deliveries add to the bill
The report puts the third-quarter price increase alongside a spike in diesel. The national average for on-highway diesel reached a record $6.53 a gallon in the week of Sept. 21, about 74% above its level a year earlier. Fuel surcharges can add to what shippers pay even when their base rates stay the same.
GEODIS also looks at what happens when a shipment arrives late or short. It points to Walmart , which charges suppliers 3% of the cost of goods on cases that miss its on-time or in-full requirements. In GEODIS’s example, a supplier shipping $100 million in goods annually would face $300,000 in penalties if late or short cases accounted for 10% of that value. Redelivery or expedited shipping can add to the bill.
Theft losses on the rise
The report flags warehouses and distribution centers as a point of exposure before the final delivery leg. GEODIS says those sites accounted for 37% of second-quarter cargo theft incidents.
In the U.S. and Canada , Verisk CargoNet recorded 677 supply chain theft incidents in the second quarter, down 26% from a year earlier. Estimated losses more than doubled to $304.6 million, driven in part by several multimillion-dollar thefts. CargoNet’s figures cover supply chain theft across transportation modes.
